subject: community-medicine
title: Cardiovascular Epidemiology: Risk Factors, Hypertension and Stroke

steps.title: Coronary heart disease risk factors and Asian phenotype
steps.tx: Cardiovascular diseases represent the leading cause of adult mortality in India, driven by the unique South Asian phenotype marked by premature onset, elevated body fat percentage at lower body mass index, central visceral adiposity and high prevalence of **coronary heart disease risk factors**. Major modifiable drivers include cigarette smoking, bidis and smokeless tobacco use, atherogenic dyslipidaemia with high triglycerides and low HDL, hypertension, diabetes mellitus and physical inactivity.
steps.say: Heart attacks strike Indians a decade earlier than Western populations due to central belly fat, diabetes, high blood pressure, tobacco smoking and low protective HDL cholesterol.

rows: Tobacco smoking, bidis, high salt, inactivity
Accounts for over 50% of preventable CVD events
High prevalence in both urban and rural cohorts
High triglycerides, low HDL, elevated Lp(a)
Classic atherogenic dyslipidaemic South Asian pattern
Advancing age, male sex, strong family history

steps.title: Hypertension classification and diagnostic criteria
steps.tx: Clinical and community guidelines establish **hypertension classification** based on standardised blood pressure readings taken after five minutes of seated rest, using an appropriately sized arm cuff. Normal adult blood pressure is defined as systolic below one hundred and twenty millimetres of mercury and diastolic below eighty; Stage 1 hypertension spans one hundred and thirty to one hundred and thirty-nine systolic or eighty to eighty-nine diastolic.
steps.say: Normal blood pressure is under one hundred and twenty over eighty. Stage one hypertension begins at one hundred and thirty systolic or eighty diastolic on repeated resting measurements.

steps.title: The rule of halves in community hypertension
steps.tx: In public health epidemiology, hypertension is famously characterized by the **rule of halves**, which illustrates substantial attrition across the clinical care pathway. Roughly half of individuals with hypertension in the population are unaware of their condition; of those diagnosed, only half receive medical treatment; and of those receiving pharmacotherapy, only half achieve adequate target blood pressure control, leaving the vast majority at risk.
steps.say: The rule of halves shows that half of hypertensive people do not know they have it. Half of those who know never take medicine, and only half of treated patients achieve normal pressure.

steps.title: Dietary salt intake and population reduction
steps.tx: Excessive sodium intake drives sustained arterial vasoconstriction, with Indian surveys revealing daily consumption exceeding ten grams, more than double the World Health Organization target of **dietary salt restriction** below five grams daily (equivalent to two grams of sodium or one level teaspoon). Population-wide salt reduction through consumer food reformulation, front-of-pack warning labels, and community awareness represents one of the most cost-effective non-communicable disease interventions.
steps.say: Indians consume over ten grams of salt each day, more than twice the recommended five-gram limit. Cutting daily salt intake lowers blood pressure across the entire community.

left.title: Current Indian salt intake
points: Average 9 to 11 grams daily per person
Sourced from added table salt, pickles, papads
Drives high rates of strokes and heart failure

right.title: WHO target recommendation
points: Less than 5 grams salt daily (<2 g sodium)
Equivalent to one level teaspoon per day

steps.title: Stroke epidemiology: ischaemic versus haemorrhagic
steps.tx: Uncontrolled hypertension acts as the pre-eminent modifiable risk factor for **cerebrovascular stroke**, precipitating both cerebral ischaemia from thromboembolism and primary intracerebral haemorrhage from ruptured Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in lenticulostriate arterioles. Ischaemic strokes account for roughly seventy-five to eighty percent of cases, while primary intracerebral haemorrhage accounts for the remaining twenty to twenty-five percent, exhibiting higher acute case fatality in lower socioeconomic rural settings.
steps.say: Hypertension is the primary cause of stroke, causing brain clots in three-quarters of patients and burst bleeding vessels in the rest. High blood pressure control directly prevents strokes.

left.title: Ischaemic stroke (75-80%)
points: Associated with atrial fibrillation, carotid atheroma

right.title: Haemorrhagic stroke (20-25%)
points: Rupture of small penetrating brain arterioles
Sudden severe headache and rapid coma
Directly caused by long-standing high blood pressure

steps.title: Acute stroke care and the golden window
steps.tx: Recognizing early stroke signs through the FAST algorithm (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency) is vital because intravenous thrombolysis must occur within the narrow **thrombolytic time window** of four point five hours from symptom onset. Primary health centres stabilize airway and blood pressure before transferring patients to district stroke units equipped with non-contrast computed tomography, avoiding premature antihypertensive over-treatment that reduces cerebral perfusion.
steps.say: Remember the FAST signs: face droop, arm weakness and slurred speech. Clot-dissolving treatment must be given within four and a half hours, making immediate hospital transfer essential.

nodes.label: Sudden onset of FAST neurological deficits
Immediate emergency transfer to stroke center
IV tissue plasminogen activator within 4.5 hours

steps.title: Rheumatic fever: streptococcal pharyngitis trigger
steps.tx: In school-aged children, untreated Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis provokes **acute rheumatic fever**, an autoimmune non-suppurative post-infectious illness triggered by molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and human cardiac myosin, synovium and basal ganglia. Symptoms erupt two to three weeks following pharyngitis, presenting with migratory polyarthritis of large joints, carditis, Sydenham chorea, subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum in overcrowded, impoverished rural homes.
steps.say: Untreated bacterial sore throat in children can trigger rheumatic fever through molecular mimicry. Antibodies attacking the bacteria mistakenly damage heart valves, joints and brain cells.

steps.title: Revised Jones criteria for rheumatic fever diagnosis
steps.tx: Clinical confirmation requires fulfilling the **revised Jones criteria**, demanding evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (elevated anti-streptolysin O titre or positive throat culture) alongside either two major criteria, or one major plus two minor criteria. Major criteria comprise carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; minor criteria include fever, arthralgia, prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
steps.say: Diagnosing rheumatic fever requires evidence of recent streptococcal infection plus two major Jones criteria, or one major criterion with two minor criteria like fever and joint pain.

rows: Positive throat swab culture for Group A Strep
Elevated ESR (>= 60 mm) or CRP (>= 3.0 mg/dl)

steps.title: Primary prevention: treating streptococcal sore throat
steps.tx: The cornerstone of preventing rheumatic fever is **primary streptococcal prevention**, ensuring prompt antibiotic eradication of Group A streptococci within nine days of sore throat onset. A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G at one point two million units for older children and adults (or oral penicillin V for ten days) completely eliminates pharyngeal streptococci, preventing initial episodes of acute rheumatic carditis entirely.
steps.say: Treating a streptococcal sore throat with a single injection of benzathine penicillin or oral penicillin for ten days cures the infection and stops rheumatic fever from ever starting.

rows: Oral azithromycin 12 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Oral erythromycin or azithromycin 500 mg daily
